question: A 24-year-old pregnant woman in her second trimester has Hb 8.2 g/dL, MCV 62 fL, low serum ferritin, and no evidence of haemorrhage. Which is the MOST appropriate first-line treatment?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Transfusion is not indicated for iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy unless Hb falls below 7 g/dL with haemodynamic compromise or near term with severe anaemia. Oral iron is safer and adequate here.

answers.text: Oral ferrous sulphate 200 mg (60 mg elemental iron) twice daily

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Oral iron is first-line for IDA in pregnancy. The standard regimen is ferrous sulphate providing ~60 mg elemental iron BD or TDS. Haemoglobin should rise by ~1 g/dL every 2–3 weeks. Continue for 3 months after Hb normalises.
Hydroxocobalamin (B12) is given for megaloblastic anaemia due to B12 deficiency. This patient has microcytic anaemia with low ferritin — classic IDA, not B12 deficiency.

Folic acid corrects folate-deficiency macrocytic anaemia and is important prophylaxis in pregnancy, but this patient's MCV of 62 fL and low ferritin point to IDA, not folate deficiency. Folic acid alone will not treat IDA.

overallFeedback.feedback: This is a classic IDA presentation: microcytic (MCV 62), hypochromic, low ferritin in a pregnant woman. First-line is oral ferrous sulphate. Transfusion is reserved for severe symptomatic anaemia close to delivery.
Well done. Oral ferrous sulphate is the cornerstone of IDA treatment in pregnancy. Track the response with a repeat Hb at 4 weeks.
